historic_survey.survey: Early Settlement Era Styles Historic Context Statement (2025)
historic_survey.note: The McElroy Octagon House, San Francisco Landmark No. 17 — an eight-sided house built in 1861. The statement counts octagon houses among the early settlement era styles but gives them no theme of their own: of at least five once standing in San Francisco, two survive, and both are city landmarks.

historical_record.description: The Octagon House, built in 1861 and one of the city's two remaining octagonal houses, was a two-story house with concrete walls covered in clapboards and an eight-sided cupola; restored by the Colonial Dames, it served as a museum of eighteenth-century antiques and was listed in the Historic American Buildings Survey. The City Planning Commission approved designating the Octagon House a city landmark under Article 10 of the Planning Code and sent the designation to the Board of Supervisors.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 17, Colonial Dames Octagon House.
Severely damaged in the 1906 earthquake, which knocked down one wall; it was repaired.

Saved from demolition by the National Society of Colonial Dames. It had passed to the Pacific Gas and Electric Company and stood empty; the Dames bought it, moved it across Gough Street from its original site at 2618 onto a lot given by the Misses Allyne, and restored it under the architect Warren Perry for their headquarters and a museum of mostly 18th-century furnishings.

unknowns: The nomination dates the house to 1861; the assessor's 2025 roll gives 1900 for the building on this parcel.

notable_residents.name: William C. McElroy
notable_residents.detail: William C. McElroy, a miller who had arrived in 1851, built the house with his wife Harriet on a lot she bought from Charles and Harry Gough, for whom the street is named; he lived here until his death in 1871 and she until 1891.

notable_residents.name: Daniel O'Connell
notable_residents.detail: The poet Daniel O'Connell lived here for about three years, when the house was a gathering place for the city's writers and artists.
